contributions.headingText: Invasive carcinoma of the male breast is a rare malignant epithelial tumour that is histologically similar to its counterpart in the female breast.

Related terminology is similar to that for invasive carcinoma of the female breast.
Male breast cancer (BC) is usually localized in the retroareolar region.

Male BC usually presents as a unilateral painless mass in the subareolar region, often slightly eccentric to the nipple. Bloody or serous discharge may be the presenting symptom. Owing to the usually small amount of mammary tissue in men, tumours can easily infiltrate the overlying skin or underlying fascia/muscle.

For men, data regarding BC carcinogenesis are limited. Male BC accounts for < 1% of all BCs {30007834} and for < 0.5% of all cancer deaths in men in the USA {26742998}. Over the last few decades, the incidence of male BC has risen in the United Kingdom, USA, Canada, Scotland, Australia, North Africa, and Middle East {18478326;26742998;31955992}, with recent data suggesting an increase in younger men. The highest incidence has been reported in Israel (1.24 cases per 100 000 person-years), which might be BRCA germline related, and the lowest in Thailand (0.16 cases per 100 000 person-years) {22987302}. Male BC is more common in Black men, in whom BC also occurs at a younger age, presents at a more-advanced stage, and is associated with higher BC-specific mortality {29050233}. Unlike the two age peaks of female BC, male BC has a single slightly older peak (median: 68.4 years) than BC in postmenopausal women {31955992}. However, it can also affect young and adolescent boys {30290658}, which is probably related to an underlying etiology that differs from female BC. Klinefelter syndrome confers a relative risk of male BC of 30–50 (as a result of increased circulating estrogen); it accounts for as many as 5% of male BCs {9494523} and is associated with a 57.8-fold increase in mortality {30290658}. Less commonly the risk of developing BC might also be influenced by hormonal changes associated with gender-affirming care, both male to female and female to male {30087072;30037639;10632490;24010586}.

Hormonal imbalance leading to a relative excess of estrogen (as seen in liver cirrhosis or Klinefelter syndrome) is the most commonly implicated cause of male BC development. As is seen with other cancers, age increases the risk of developing BC in men. Obesity has also been linked to the disease, with an increase in body mass index having a significant effect {24552677;26044503}. Cryptorchidism, mumps, orchitis, testicular trauma, and prostate cancer also increase the risk of male BC {23425944}.

Approximately 20% of male patients with BC have a first-degree family member with BC {11879560}. Men with a family history of female or male BC have a 2–3 times increased risk of developing breast carcinoma. One third of familial male BCs seem to arise in carriers of BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations, with the remainder associated with other genes (e.g. CHEK2 and PALB2), whereas other cases have unknown underlying genetic mechanisms {26857456}. Mutations and rearrangements of BRCA2 are more frequent than those of BRCA1 in male BC, and for carriers of BRCA2 variants, the risk of developing BC is 80 times that in the general population {34458944}. About 5–10% of male carriers of BRCA2 variants develop BC in their lifetime {23425944}, compared with 1–2% of BRCA1 variant carriers. Male BCs related to BRCA1/BRCA2 variants display pathological characteristics distinct from those of female BCs related to BRCA1/BRCA2 variants, and they show a more aggressive phenotype {26857456}.

Environmental factors such as ionizing radiation and electromagnetic exposure, alcohol consumption, smoking, and red meat consumption have been linked to increased male BC incidence {26694922}. Most studies have found no convincing causative link between gynaecomastia and male BC.

The precise pathogenesis is not fully understood, but genetic, hormonal, and environmental factors are thought to lead to hormonal imbalance, with a relative excess of estrogen-to-androgen ratio, causing enhanced proliferation of mammary epithelial cells. Several recently published molecular studies {26960396;20625818} show differences between male and female BC, with proportionately more luminal cancers in male than female patients and almost half the proportion of HER2-enriched, basal, and triple-negative subtypes among male BC compared with female BCs {23146383;22056953}. Whole-genome sequencing data has identified potential therapeutic targets including high tumour mutation burden, FGFR1 amplification, and homologous recombination deficiency {38369186}.

The pattern of chromosomal gains and losses in ER-positive male BC is similar to that of ER-positive female BC, except for gains on the X chromosome in male BC. A substantial proportion of male BCs have a BRCA2-like profile {26355282} and are generally enriched for mutations in DNA repair–related genes {26960396}. Male BC shows more frequent CCND1 amplification, fewer copy-number changes on chromosome 17 {25906114}, and less frequent copy-number loss on 16q {23743929;22527098}. Mutations in PIK3CA and TP53 found in female ER-positive, HER2-negative tumours {23971979} are less frequent in male BC {39049124}. The role of AR as a driver gene in male BC {20625818} has been well established. AR is highly expressed in male BC {25941088;26475094}, with X chromosome aneusomy and consequent AR polysomy described in about 74% of cases {29802469}. These data are consistent with the recent observation of the value of antiandrogen therapy in male BC {28062545}.

mRNA expression profiling in male BC shows minimal overlap with female BC {22333393;20625818;24194916}. There is frequent activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR {23971979} and FGFR2 pathways in male BC, a finding which may provide promising future targets for therapy. There are similarities and differences in methylated genes in male BC compared with female BC, with lower methylation rates in male BC overall {16401708;22765268} but relatively frequent ESR1 and GSTP1 methylation in high-grade male BC {22765268}. There are only limited data on a limited number of microRNAs in male BC, but again these differ from those in female BC {20331864;19664288}.
Male BC usually forms a large stellate or nodular mass, which may also involve the nipple.

The most common type of invasive male BC is invasive ductal carcinoma of no special type (NST). Unlike in female BC, the second most common tumour is papillary carcinoma. Invasive lobular carcinoma and other special types, such as mucinous, tubular, and metaplastic carcinomas, are extremely rare. BRCA2-associated male BCs have a lower frequency of lobular carcinomas and are more likely to be of higher grade and stage, hormone receptor–positive, and node-positive than BRCA2-associated female BCs {26857456}. Most tumours are grade 2 {28350011;23146383}. In high-grade male BC, a fibrotic focus may be found {22684218;24457463}.

Male BC is usually ER-positive and/or PR-positive (> 90% of cases) {28350011;22958056}, with frequent AR expression {25738829}. HER2-low expression is frequently seen in male BC {38562651;38339299;39410019}.

HER2-positive, triple-negative, and basal-like tumours are rare {22094935;23146383;22958056} and therefore metastases to the male breast (such as metastatic prostate cancer, which is positive for PSA, PSMA, and NKX3-1) should be considered on encountering such profiles, particularly in the absence of DCIS. Typical markers of breast epithelium, such as GATA3, cyclin D1, mammaglobin, BCL2, and GCDFP-15 (BRST2), are expressed in most male BCs and maintained in metastases {29116378;22958056}. Recently, TRPS1 has been shown to be a sensitive and specific marker for male BC that is uncommonly expressed in metastases to the male breast {37331526}.

Sentinel node and axillary clearance specimens are reported using the same guidelines as for female BC.
The features of invasive carcinoma in the male breast are the same as those in female patients {22246937}.

Essential: an invasive carcinoma with evidence of breast epithelial origin on morphology; with or without immunohistochemistry; invasive breast carcinoma NST when pure special subtypes, if present, constitute < 10% and mixed invasive breast carcinoma NST and special type carcinoma when it constitutes between 10% and 90%.

The ninth edition of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM classification [[Brierley JD, Giuliani M, O’Sullivan B, et al., editors. TNM classification of malignant tumours. 9th ed. Oxford (UK): John Wiley & Sons; 2025. ]] should be used as for female BC.

Data from the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) 10085/TBCRC/BIG/NABCG International Male BC Program demonstrate that most patients with male BC present with T1 (48.7%) or T2 (38.3%) disease. There is axillary lymph node metastasis in 40.6% of cases, with low-volume nodal involvement (N1: 32.2%, N2: 5.3%, and N3: 3%) {28292559}. Distant metastases at presentation have been reported in a small proportion of cases (5.1%) {29092024}.

Disease outcome is influenced by stage, hormone receptor status, mitotic count, grade, molecular subtype, and nodal status {22684218;22056953;22527098;22765268;22958056;23573235;28292559}. Nodal positivity has an adverse effect on disease-free survival and overall survival {28350011}. HER2 low expression has no prognostic impact but it could be a guide for therapy especially in metastatic settings {38562651;38339299;39410019}. Despite contradictory data, the general understanding is that male BC has a prognosis similar to that of female BC with equivalent stage and patient age {26313461;29050233;30007834;23341341}. Globally, except for Latin America, the age-adjusted mortality from male BC decreased between 10% and 40% in north-west Europe, Russia, and the US between 2000–2004 and 2015–2017 {33470692}. It has been suggested that married patients have a significantly longer 5-year survival rate, indicating the importance of spousal support {29795054}.

There are few if any prognostic markers, owing to the low numbers of male BCs reported. Nevertheless, as with female BC, hormone receptor expression and HER2 status are used as predictors of therapy response. Prognostic models applied in female BC, such as the Nottingham Prognostic Index (NPI) and Predict, can also be of practical management value in male BC {27671991}. The role of grading performed according to the criteria followed in female BC has been challenged {28292559}, because thresholds for mitotic count may differ. The application of genomic tests is still limited in male BC. However, currently published data indicate a potential benefit in their use to guide treatment planning {31588557;32472417;31748278}. A BRCA2-like profile may indicate benefit from targeted therapy, as seen in female BC {26355282}.

A recent analysis of the SEER data compared the molecular differences and outcomes between male and female BC after adjusting for confounders. Distinct differences in the transcriptomes, genomes, epigenomes, and immune microenvironment were identified accounting for poorer prognosis of male BC. Male BC strongly expressed five proteins that promote BC progression, was less immunogenic with comparatively poorer response to immunotherapy, and showed a more pronounced effect of estrogen. In addition, six therapeutic target genes approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) were differentially expressed between the cancers {38701649}.
